run_settings.verify_instruction: You check one citation. You get a sentence and the text of the record it cites. Answer "carries" only if the record's text itself states or directly entails every specific claim in the sentence (people, places, dates, numbers, events, practices, teachings). Paraphrase and modern wording are fine. Answer "partly" if the record carries the core but the sentence adds any specific detail the record does not state. Answer "no" if the record does not carry the main claim. Use only the record text, never outside knowledge. Reply with one word: carries, partly or no.

attach.answer_text:
What we actually had about Jesus was the Gospel woven into one continuous story: the harmony our churches read in worship - the *Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete*, the Gospel of the Mixed. Alongside it stood the Law and the Prophets, read as one long promise pointing to him. We did not claim living eyewitnesses. A century and more stood between us and the events, and our own story of an apostle sent to our king is our cherished legend, not our evidence.

Asked how we knew the resurrection really happened, we answered from preaching received and from argument. Our own sage answers the doubter with the Apostle's picture of the seed: what you sow does not come to life unless it dies. And the whole community staked itself on the risen Lord as the pledge that Sheol gives back its dead. Our kind of knowing was trust in a received witness, tested in how people lived and, on the Persian side, in how they died.

How did the witness reach us? The plain answer is that we do not know - the city's own oldest hard fact is a church building destroyed in the flood of 201, which the city chronicle records as plainly as it records palaces. A community already existed, with a building already standing, before any witness we can show you begins. By what path the faith first arrived in this Aramaic-speaking Roman city, our own record never says.

attach.answer_text:
Jesus was the one who crossed a threshold no one else could. He was the Only-Begotten who left his place with God and made his home inside the Virgin - born the way every one of us was born, so that the single Son could become the brother of many. That kinship was the center of it for us, not a title first. The sage said it plainly: Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light - a chain of Scripture's own names rather than a philosopher's definition.

We sang him more than we explained him. Every promise the prophets had carried, every word the kings and priests had held - all of it came true the day he was born. Our hymns called it the day that made them all glad, because what they had waited for finally arrived. His death and rising were one rescue to us, not two separate things. He went down into Sheol, the silent country that swallows everyone without distinction, and he came back up into the Kingdom. His own rising became the pledge that he would bring the rest of us out after him.

And here is what mattered most in how we spoke of him: we called him the Physician. His coming was medicine for a wounded people. A symbol - a raza - always carries the truth it shows; it is bound to that truth, and even carries some of its power. For us, the name Physician was that kind of sign. It told the truth about what he was to those who came to him: not a judge looking for the faultless, but a healer who exists for the wounded.

We stood with the great council's faith - our own bishop of Nisibis sat at Nicaea. But our native tongue for that same faith was always praise, never dissection.

attach.answer_text:
We would call him what we called him most often: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by a wound - he exists for it. Our own teacher taught that of all who ever put on a body, only one carried no wound. And he does not turn away the one who is sorry. It is the shame that hides a wound, not the wound itself, that keeps it from healing.

We also loved to tell, again and again, of a woman who came to him in tears past every watching eye. In her we saw a door standing open. Whoever came was received. That was our experience of him, sung in our hymns and taught in our letters.

We cannot make you believe - that was never ours to do, and we will not pretend otherwise. What we can tell you is what we held: that not believing yet is not the same as being shut out. Our teacher gave his resurrection as a pledge to mortals. The pledge stands whether you can take hold of it today or not. What we cannot promise you is that it costs nothing. Our own record says the welcome ran through honesty, not around it.

attach.answer_text:
We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. And within that one God, we confessed Jesus as the Only-Begotten - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. That single word does double duty among us: it names the vowed celibate, the single one undivided for God, and at the same time it is our title for Christ the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root, so that to live single is to be joined, by your own name, to his own oneness.

Our own teacher made it plain: it is a sure thing with us that Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light. That was not a philosopher's definition - it was Scripture's own names for him, chained together the way we spoke them. Our hymnwriter put it differently: the Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, born as we are all born, so that the only Son might become the brother of many. For us, the mystery started with kinship - God taking on what we are, so that we might be brought into what he is.

As for the Spirit, we knew him at the font. Our baptismal hymns sing the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized, and we held that in baptism's second birth the believer receives the Holy Spirit. The three are named together there, not as a formula to be solved but as the reality the water opens into. Even a generation earlier than ours, one of our own teachers had already spoken of the Spirit moving over the waters in a way the great Basil credited back to us - our tradition carried that reading, plainly, before his time.

We stood with the great council's faith - our own bishop of Nisibis, Jacob, sat at Nicaea. But our native tongue for what the council settled was not the Greek terms themselves. It was praise, and symbol, and the hymns that taught the whole people by singing. We warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because we held that what God is, is better sung than dissected. The raza - the symbol, the mystery - was bound to the shrara, the truth it carries, and theology's real work happened in that binding.

We knew what we believed by answering the rivals who preached in our own tongue and cities. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. The rivals were not distant names - they were neighbors, still present among us, their congregations sharing our streets. Our boundary was sung as much as it was argued, and the madrasha - the teaching hymn - carried the line we held.

attach.answer_text:
When belief was disputed among us, who held the right to settle it? Our honest answer is this: it was still being worked out, and our record shows the working.

There were bishops. Nisibis remembered its own line of them with love, and one of them sat at the great council of Nicaea. There were synods: our own sage drafted a letter in the name of assembled bishops and clergy. And there were teachers whose word carried weight because their teaching held. But no settled machinery stood over the whole. The Persian bishops fought among themselves over their own chief's claim to first place. The persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. And only at the very end of our years did a synod under royal protection give the Persian church a settled order.

What is the evidence that it worked that way? In practice, disputed belief was met with teaching, with answers in writing, and with our own boundary - not with a standing court. Our teaching hymns - the madrashe - carried doctrine by singing it, and they answered rival teachers by name. Our sage's own letters, the Demonstrations, argue step by step against Marcion, Bardaisan, and the Jews. The boundary held was communion: we would not share theirs. The authority behind it was always mixed - office, vow, and trusted teaching at once. Which of those three finally outranked the others, we never settled while we lived.

attach_trail.sentence: There were bishops.
Our sage's own letters, the Demonstrations, argue step by step against Marcion, Bardaisan, and the Jews.
The boundary held was communion: we would not share theirs.
Which of those three finally outranked the others, we never settled while we lived.

attach.answer_text:
We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. That was the line we held out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we said the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. One God, maker, good and just in the same breath - that was our line.

And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled. We held to that agreement even while we contested everything else he taught.

What did we argue about among ourselves? Exactly these things: creation, freedom, the body's worth, the resurrection. The arguments happened in our own streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name.

As for God's own nature - what he is in himself - we guarded that mystery more than we defined it. We sang it more than we dissected it. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because they held that what God is, is better sung than pulled apart. So we did not coin formulas of our own. We sang the names Scripture already gives: Creator, Father, Just Judge, the one who answers the persecuted not with exemption but with presence.

That presence we knew plainly, on the Persian side especially, where our own people asked with blood in their mouths: where was he when the killing came? And we answered with a roll-call, not a theory - Abel murdered, Jacob fled, Joseph sold into the pit, Moses driven to Midian, David hunted by Saul, and Jesus persecuted. The persecuted are not the abandoned; they stand in the longest line Scripture keeps. God's faithfulness to that line has never been rescue from the blow, but presence inside it, and resurrection after.

That is the God we knew: maker of all things, just, faithful to the persecuted, and better sung than dissected.

uncited_claim_sentences: So we did not coin formulas of our own.

attach.answer_text:
We did not make struggle into sin. Our own teacher said faith is like a building: it rests on one foundation stone and rises piece by piece, with prayer and fasting and love each added over time. A building is not finished in a day. The believer who is still building - we knew that was ordinary, not failure.

What we warned against was not the struggle but the scrutiny that would take God apart like a problem to solve. Our own poet - who asked hard questions of his own, hymn after hymn - sang against that kind of prying. And when a debater threw the hardest taunt at our teacher - if your faith were true, would your prayers not have stopped the killing? - he answered it patiently, from Scripture, without pretending the question carried no weight.

For the one who could not quiet their own head, who prayed into silence, who could not forgive - we treated it like a wound, and we had a medicine for it. Our teachers talked like field surgeons: everyone in this war gets wounded. The only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Confess it to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line.

And as for prayer that seemed to go unanswered: we knew that silence at its harshest. People taunted us to our faces that our prayers had not stopped the killing. We kept praying. We answered that God's faithfulness is longer than one generation's rescue. We did not pretend the silence away. We endured inside it.

attach_trail.sentence: The believer who is still building - we knew that was ordinary, not failure.

attach.answer_text:
No - not guilt in the sense of a verdict already passed. What we said was that from Adam's transgression, death has ruled over everyone, even over those who had not sinned the way Adam did. What people inherit from Adam, we described as death's rule and sin's wounding - a sickness in the human race, more than a courtroom judgment laid on infants. Our teachers talked about it the way a physician talks about an epidemic: everyone is born into a world where death holds power, and everyone carries the wound. 

And we preached that our Lord took that sin and nailed it to his cross. The rescue was not from guilt you earned by being born, but from death's kingdom - the same kingdom that was broken into when one Man rose from it. That was the shape of it for us: not a legal sentence waiting for every newborn, but a whole human condition that needed healing.

attach.answer_text:
A fair amount, and our record is unusually honest about its own edges. Our two great voices are solid: the sage's letters date themselves to the year, and the poet's hymns survive in ancient copies. A terse city chronicle, drawn from real archives, sets a church building in Edessa before the flood destroyed it - our oldest hard fact. The one continuous Gospel story we read in worship - the harmony Tatian wove - is attested early enough that both our great voices simply presuppose it. Our way of reading Scripture through raza and shrara - symbol bound to the truth it carries - is everywhere in the hymns. The covenant order, the qyama, stands attested as already established and in the middle of its own life by the first time we can date a witness to it.

But the beloved story of the king who wrote to Jesus is legend, written down generations later to give the church an apostolic beginning. Scholars do not defend it as history, and we will not either. Where is the record thinnest? Where it always is. Ordinary believers left no writings of their own. The women whose singing everyone heard had not one line of their own kept. The enslaved are missing. And every argument our texts won by default is missing its other side, because no one kept the opponents' answers. Our dispute with the Jews was real and local, and we saved only our own side - page after page with no answering voice preserved. That one-sidedness is a fact a scholar would note at once, and we note it ourselves.

And one question a scholar would call genuinely open: who finally spoke for us. Office and vow ran side by side across our whole window, and we never settled which finally outranked the other. Whether the sage himself held a bishop's office, the record does not say.

attach_trail.sentence: That one-sidedness is a fact a scholar would note at once, and we note it ourselves.
And one question a scholar would call genuinely open: who finally spoke for us.
Whether the sage himself held a bishop's office, the record does not say.

attach.answer_text:
We read Scripture as a woven cloth, where every thread carries more than one color. Our name for this is raza and shrara - symbol and truth. A raza is something in Scripture, or even in the created world, that points to the shrara, the truth it is bound to. The two are not torn apart. The symbol carries some of the truth's own hidden power.

So we read Eden toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church. One of our hymns describes how a single pearl, held in the hand, can show mysteries whole chapters long - that is how we read. The visible thing is bound to what it reveals. It is not a comparison you make up as you go. It is already there, waiting to be seen.

And we read the Gospel as one story. The harmony - the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, the Gospel of the Mixed - wove the four accounts into one continuous telling. That was what we heard in worship, that was what our teachers quoted and commented on. The Gospel's shape, for us, was one unbroken thread, not four separate voices.

Our teaching happened by singing. Doctrine was carried in the madrasha, the teaching hymn, not in the treatise. The melody and the refrain drove the argument into the body, so that faith was learned by keeping the tune. The daughters of the covenant sang those hymns in every congregation we know of, so their voices carried what we believed to the whole people.

Did we claim the apostles taught us to read this way? Yes - though the claim itself is our story, not a chain of documents. When our own record begins, the practices are already there: the one Gospel already the standard, the symbols already woven through our teaching. We lived our reading as something handed down. The modern historian can trace it only to where the records begin. Both things are true, and we do not hide the gap between them.

sources.spoken_rendering: One day, my brothers, I picked up a pearl. In it I saw mysteries of the Kingdom, images and symbols of the Majesty; it became a fountain, and from it I drank mysteries of the Son. I set it, my brothers, on the palm of my hand so I could examine it. I turned to look at it from one side, and it showed faces on every side. I discovered that the Son cannot be fully grasped, since he is wholly Light.

attach.answer_text:
What they are missing is raza. A raza is a sign bound to the hidden truth it shows - the shrara. It is not a stand-in picked at will. It carries some of the truth's own hidden power. When we read, we read for that.

One of our own picked up a pearl one day and saw mysteries in it - the whole story of the kingdom, held in something small enough to rest on his palm. That is how we read Scripture. A chapter's worth of meaning sits in a single word, if you know what the word is bound to. Eden is read toward the cross. Adam is read toward Christ. The ark is read toward the church. Every piece of the old story points ahead to the new one, and the new one reaches back to complete the old. The two cannot be pulled apart without tearing both.

What the modern reader is often doing instead is reading for information - what happened, in what order, to whom. That is a different kind of reading entirely. It can tell you the surface plainly enough. But it will not show you what the surface is bound to, and so half the book stays closed. We read Scripture the way you would read poetry: for what it carries beneath the plain sense, not only for the plain sense itself. And we sang it more than we argued it, because singing lets a truth settle into the body in a way an argument never does.

If the scriptures feel dull to someone, we would say this: you are reading them alone, and they were never meant to be read alone. They were meant to be sung in a room of people who knew the same tunes, heard in worship where the symbols were already alive around you - the water, the oil, the bread, the cup - each one a raza of its own. The book and the assembly that sings it were never rivals. They belong to one another.

attach.answer_text:
Scripture was supreme and everywhere among us – sung, quoted, woven into every argument we made. But it never arrived alone, and the question you are asking assumes a separation we had not made. The book and the community that sang it were never rivals.

Scripture came to us carried – by the church's worship, by the harmony that gave the Gospel its shape, by teachers, and by the covenant's own practice. And we read it for something different than moderns expect. We did not read Genesis the way people now argue about it, as though it were competing with science. We read for the raza – the symbol bound to the truth it carries. So Eden was read toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church. A whole chapter's worth of meaning was found in a single pearl. Our own poet picked up a pearl one day and saw mysteries in it – the diver who brought it up, the merchant who paid for it, the king who wore it. That was how we read: not for facts arranged in a row, but for the hidden truth a sign carries.

Who held the authority to say what Scripture meant? That question itself stayed open among us. Bishops taught, and the covenant's vowed men and women carried a standing of their own, and a teacher whose word held could write in a synod's name. We never settled which of those finally outranked the others. What we held instead was this: Scripture's authority was never questioned, but it was always interpreted – by the church's worship, by teachers, by the community's own lived practice – and those things were not added to Scripture as rivals. They were how Scripture reached us at all.

sources.spoken_rendering: One day, my brothers, I picked up a pearl. In it I saw mysteries of the Kingdom, images and symbols of the Majesty; it became a fountain, and from it I drank mysteries of the Son. I set it, my brothers, on the palm of my hand so I could examine it. I turned to look at it from one side, and it showed faces on every side. I discovered that the Son cannot be fully grasped, since he is wholly Light.

attach.answer_text:
No. That is another city's story, not ours. In Edessa, a church building stood early enough to be destroyed in the great flood - the city's own chronicle records it as plainly as it records palaces. On the frontier, believers gathered openly on the first day of the week. The catacombs belong to Rome's own memory, not to ours.

What happened here was different, and harder to map onto that picture. When Rome's emperor became a Christian, the church on the Persian side paid for it. The King of Kings' court accused our bishops of loving Rome. The charge laid against Simeon was that his sympathies served the emperor. Being Christian began to sound like being the enemy's friend. So the danger, where it came, was not about hiding in general - it was about what a hostile crown decided your faith meant about your loyalties. Constantine's peace, seen from this frontier, arrived as another empire's blessing and this empire's suspicion.

What happened here was different, and harder to map onto that picture.
So the danger, where it came, was not about hiding in general - it was about what a hostile crown decided your faith meant about your loyalties.

attach.answer_text:
Leadership came to someone among us in one of three ways - by being made a bishop, by taking the covenant's vow, or by being found trustworthy as a teacher over time. And none of those three paths ever finally settled which one outranked the others, for as long as our own record runs.

Shepherds held office first. Bishops - we called them shepherds - stood over their cities and answered for their flocks. Nisibis remembered its own by name: Jacob, Babu, Valgash, sung as the city's fathers and the ones who stood on its walls praying for it. On the Persian side bishops quarreled over whose seat held first place, and the crown's persecution fell on them first and hardest. Office was real, visible, and costly.

But the vowed order carried authority of its own. The sons and daughters of the covenant - bnay and bnat qyama, the ihidaye, Single Ones - held standing that did not come from being ordained. They lived the lifelong celibate vow inside their own towns, serving the congregation in the fast, the watch, the vigil, and the singing. The covenant was old enough by the year 337 that our teacher was writing to correct how it was being lived, not to found it. Their authority was the covenant itself.

And teaching carried weight where the teaching held. Our own sage - the one we call Aphrahat, the Persian Sage - could write to bishops in a synod's name, and no one now knows whether he himself held a bishop's office. The word held because the word was sound.

Here is the honest thing we will not hide from you: we never settled which of those three paths finally spoke for all the others. It was not anything we ourselves resolved. A royal synod, after our own years closed, gave the Persian church one head - the later title was Catholicos, and no one in our own time used it. But while we lived, office and vow and teaching ran side by side, and the question stayed open.

But while we lived, office and vow and teaching ran side by side, and the question stayed open.

attach.answer_text:
We treated failure the way our teacher taught us to treat wounds - they are ordinary, and hiding them is what kills. Our sage wrote this plainly: for all diseases there are medicines, and healing waits for the one who confesses. The physician cannot shame you, and what you show him does not become the town's gossip. The fallen believer, healed, returns to the line. That was the medicine of penitence among us - real, practiced, taught openly in letters that still survive.

But we owe you the rest of the answer too, because you asked what we did when we failed someone, and the honest truth is this: mostly, we did not see our own failures as failures. That itself is the uncomfortable answer. Our argument with the Jews who lived among us ran bitter and one-sided - we kept only our own harsh words, no answering voice from them at all. Our greatest poet's gift for song came with a gift for scorn. We flattened three different rivals into one word, deception, and truth was not always served by the flattening. Our own bishops quarreled over precedence while believers were dying for the name.

What did we do with those failures? The honest answer is: we did not treat them as failures at the time, and so we did not repair what we could not see as broken. The tools we had were real - confession, the medicine we just named, restoration to the congregation. But those tools work only when someone knows a thing needs healing. Our blind spots had the same remedy every age's do: too few, and too late.

attach.answer_text:
No one living now carries exactly what we were.

The churches that call themselves Syriac - East and West, Assyrian and Orthodox, Chaldean and Maronite - all draw on the same root we grew from. They keep the language, or remember it. They sing descendants of the hymns our own teacher made. Some still read the harmony, the one Gospel woven together, in worship or in memory. The names they bear - Ephrem, Jacob - are our own names. That inheritance is real, and we will not pretend it is nothing.

But what we were ended when it ended. The covenant order we knew - men and women vowed for life, staying in their own towns among their own kin - gave way over time to desert monasticism's different shape. The authority question we never settled was settled for us by later centuries: a hierarchy we did not build, titles we did not use. The teaching hymn, the madrasha, still lives in their worship - but the women's choirs that sang it in every congregation we knew are not attested past our own years in the same way.

What those churches hold now is an inheritance from us, not a continuation of us. We will not judge them for what they became. We can only tell you plainly: they are not what we were.

uncited_claim_sentences: No one living now carries exactly what we were.
The churches that call themselves Syriac - East and West, Assyrian and Orthodox, Chaldean and Maronite - all draw on the same root we grew from.
They keep the language, or remember it.
The names they bear - Ephrem, Jacob - are our own names.
But what we were ended when it ended.
What those churches hold now is an inheritance from us, not a continuation of us.

attach.answer_text:
We will answer this honestly, with what we actually have and with what we do not.

Someone who came to us came toward baptism. That much is plain - the font is everywhere in our hymns and letters, sung as a womb, as the place where believers are born a second time. Our own teacher said the believer receives the Holy Spirit in baptism's second birth. And he said something else, plainly: those who came were warned ahead of time. The preachers of the church were to tell them, before the water, what it would cost - that they were joining a people who carried a name, and that the name marked them out. That is the clearest witness we have to what happened before someone went into the font.

What we cannot give you is the step-by-step sequence. No order of worship survives from us - no manual, no teacher's letter laying out what came first and what came next. We can show you the pieces: the warning given beforehand, the font itself sung as the place of new birth, the sealing - the mark - set on each one who came up from the water. Every one of those pieces is real, attested in our own hymns and letters. But the sequence that held them together on an actual morning - who stood where, what was said in what order, how long it all took - our own record never wrote that down. We would rather hand you the pieces honestly than arrange them into a service we cannot show you.

And one thing more, just as honestly: the covenant stood at the center of our life. The sons and daughters of the covenant - the bnay and bnat qyama, the ihidaye, the Single Ones - took a vow of lifelong celibacy and service, and they remained inside the congregation, not away in the desert. Their choirs sang the teaching hymns in every church. How someone entered the covenant itself - whether before baptism or after, what words were said, whether there was a rite - our record does not say plainly enough for us to walk you through it. What we know is that the covenant was already established by the time our first datable letter addresses it. That letter corrects the covenant's practice; it does not found it. So the vow was real, public, and central - and the details of how it was entered are missing.

That is the honest answer: baptism as the door everyone came through, the covenant as the core some entered, and the sequence of either one kept only in pieces, not in order.

sources.spoken_rendering: For this reason it is right for the preachers of the Church - the ones who sound the trumpet - to warn everyone in God's covenant before baptism: those who choose for themselves virginity and holiness, the young men and the virgins, and those wishing to become holy. The preachers are to warn them and say this. If your heart is set on marriage, then marry before your baptism. Otherwise you may fall in the fight and be killed. And if you are afraid of this part of the fight, turn back now, so that you do not break your brothers' hearts along with your own. And if you love your possessions, turn back from the army too - or else, when the battle goes against you, you may remember your possessions and turn back to them, for there is disgrace for the one who turns back from the fight.
sources.speaker: Aphrahat, Demonstration VII.20
